blogs.title: IMNM vs. Rhabdomyolysis: When CK Elevation Isn't What It Seems
blogs.description: This post will break down the critical clinical and temporal distinctions between immune-mediated necrotising myopathy (IMNM) and drug-induced rhabdomyolysis—two entities that both present with CK elevation and weakness but demand radically different management. Using the contrast between this case (semaglutide-associated IMNM with a 12-fold CK rise over 4 months and requirement for immunosuppression) and the previously reported tirzepatide-associated rhabdomyolysis (CK of 57,014 with rapid resolution on drug withdrawal and hydration alone), we will explore how timeline, CK trajectory, histologic features, and response to withdrawal vs. immunosuppression can help clinicians tell these apart at the bedside.

blogs.title: GLP-1 Receptor Agonists and Skeletal Muscle: Beyond the GI Side Effects We Talk About
blogs.description: With GLP-1 receptor agonists exploding in popularity for obesity and type 2 diabetes, this post will examine the emerging— and underappreciated—spectrum of skeletal muscle adverse effects associated with this drug class. We will review what is currently known (muscle mass loss, a reported case of tirzepatide-associated rhabdomyolysis, and now this first probable case of semaglutide-associated IMNM), discuss the pharmacovigilance implications of detecting rare autoimmune adverse effects in widely prescribed medications, and consider what predisposing factors might put patients at risk. The post will also draw parallels to how statin-associated IMNM was initially missed and only later recognized, raising the question: are we at the beginning of a similar recognition curve for GLP-1 agonists?

blogs.title: The Seronegative Myopathy Dilemma: When the Autoantibody Panel Comes Back Empty
blogs.description: This post will focus on the diagnostic challenge posed by seronegative IMNM, which accounts for an estimated one-third of cases. Using this patient's completely negative myositis panel (including anti-HMGCR and anti-SRP) as a springboard, we will discuss how clinicians should approach a patient with progressive proximal weakness, significant CK elevation, and no identifiable autoantibody. Key topics will include the role of muscle biopsy in confirming necrotising myopathy, the histologic hallmarks that distinguish IMNM from polymyositis and toxic myopathy, and the clinical reasoning that allows a diagnosis of IMNM even in the absence of serologic confirmation. We will also address how a weakly positive SS-B antibody with negative ANA and SS-A fits—or doesn't fit—into the diagnostic picture.

blogs.title: Drug-Induced vs. Idiopathic IMNM: Does the Trigger Change the Treatment Plan?
blogs.description: This post will explore whether drug-induced IMNM can be treated with shorter, less intensive immunosuppressive regimens compared to idiopathic IMNM, which typically requires prolonged and aggressive immunosuppression. The case patient received pulse methylprednisolone, oral prednisone, and a single course of IVIG—and was successfully weaned off all immunosuppression within 2 months, remaining in remission at 10 months. We will discuss the clinical reasoning behind expecting a more self-limited course when the offending agent is withdrawn, how to balance sufficient immunosuppression against the risks of prolonged therapy, and whether the approach to statin-associated HMGCR-positive IMNM (which often requires ongoing treatment despite statin cessation) offers a contrasting lesson about trigger removal vs. self-limited disease.

blogs.title: Myositis and the Heart: Making Sense of Cardiac Findings in Inflammatory Myopathy
blogs.description: This post will tackle the often-confusing cardiac findings encountered in patients with inflammatory myopathies, using this case's mildly elevated high-sensitivity troponin (62 pg/mL), markedly elevated proBNP (4358 pg/mL), echocardiographic pulmonary hypertension estimate, and cardiac MRI showing myocardial edema with mid-anteroseptal hypokinesis without late gadolinium enhancement. We will discuss the differential diagnosis (active myocarditis vs. stress-induced cardiomyopathy vs. troponin elevation from skeletal muscle injury), the limitations of troponin as a cardiac-specific marker in the setting of severe myopathy, and how to interpret ambiguous cardiac MRI findings. The post will also review the clinical significance of cardiac involvement in IMNM specifically and how follow-up imaging can help clarify the etiology of initial cardiac abnormalities.
